newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia sets up first privatisation ministry.
newsitem.headline: Serbia sets up first privatisation ministry.

text.p: The Serbian government named businessman Milan Beko to head a new ministry that will begin the privatisation of the huge state sector of the economy.

To allay public disquiet, Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic told parliament that the Ministry for Ownership Transformation would be coupled with a safety net to protect society from the effects of market reforms.

"The government will not allow the burden of market reforms to fall on the economically weakest section of the population," he added on Tuesday. "We will prepare a comprehensive programme of social protection to ease the burden on workers."
Marjanovic described privatisation of companies and banks as an enormous challenge that would lead to healthy market competition.

Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic decided last month to go ahead with privatisation as part of his Socialist government's efforts to revive the economy crippled by U.N. sanctions and the collapse of former Yugoslavia.

Serbia's economy has remained tightly centralised under government control in contrast with other central and eastern European economies which have undergone rapid transformation since the fall of communist rule in 1989-90.

Some of the country's biggest companies are headed by Socialist government ministers who resisted privatisation, fearing that economic liberalisation would weaken the political grip of the Socialist party and its allies.

Political sources said Milosevic had been forced to act now because of the need to establish conditions for Serbia's return to international respectability after almost three months of street protests against socialist election rigging.
Although 3-1/2 years of sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia during the war in Bosnia have been lifted, Serbia is still shut out of international financial and diplomatic institutions.
The Serbian government is due to pass a privatisation law in April.
Federal Yugoslav privatisation legislation passed a year ago was regarded as ineffectual, leaving it to state companies themselves to decide whether to transform themselves.

Plans are currently being made to privatise the Serbian PTT and the Zastava industrial conglomerate but economists fear the proceeds will be used to plug deficits in public spending rather than be devoted to economic development.
